newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF, Swiss authorities discuss eurobond ID plan - MOF.
newsitem.headline: MOF, Swiss authorities discuss eurobond ID plan - MOF.

text.p: Japanese and Swiss financial officials are discussing ways of adopting an identification system for holders of foreign bonds issued by Japanese firms which meets Japanese tax requirements and Swiss financial traditions, a Ministry of Finance official said on Friday.

The official said the ministry is considering requiring that a purchaser of such bonds in the Swiss market be identified only once, at the time of purchase, but this would need the cooperation of the Swiss government.
MOF's original plan was to have the custodian of foreign bonds issued by Japanese firms identify the bond holder each time a coupon payment is made.

"We are considering easing our identification scheme so it matches the characteristics of the Swiss market," he said. "We are still in a process of exchanging opinions with monetary and banking officials there."
He said the plan would need the cooperation of the Swiss government to ensure that the purchasers were identified.

MOF has been saying it would keep in mind the special characteristics of the Swiss financial market, which adheres to strict rules of confidentiality, after Swiss banks strongly opposed MOF's original plan when it was first disclosed last October.
The contentious scheme reflects MOF's long-standing desire to close a tax loophole.
MOF allows a tax break on income gains on foreign bonds, including eurobonds, issued by Japanese firms held by non-Japanese residents.
However, according to MOF, local investors are taking advantage of the tax break intended for foreigners to avoid paying taxes.
A MOF study showed that 70 to 80 percent of such bonds are held by Japanese investors.
MOF has said it wants to prepare a bill to close the loophole so it can be approved by an extraordinary parliament session to be held this autumn.
If it is approved then, it would be effective in the fiscal year which starts next April, but Japanese issuers, underwriters and other industries are still demanding that MOF modify the plan.
